questions.question: Q1. In the Ashby weighted sum M_total = w_1·M̂_1 + w_2·M̂_2 + w_3·M̂_3, what is the mathematical consequence of using a linear combination rather than a multiplicative function (e.g., product)?

answers.a: The product would give negative scores.
answers.b: The linear sum cannot capture property trade-offs (e.g. stiff materials being brittle).
answers.c: Linear sums are required by the NASA standard.

explanations.a: Incorrect - Products can be positive; the issue is not sign but expressiveness.
explanations.b: Correct - A linear weighted sum is a screening tool that ignores correlations between properties; real materials often have coupled strengths and weaknesses. This is why the capstone explicitly notes it as a first-pass filter, not the final design decision.
explanations.c: Incorrect - NASA/ISRO standards do not mandate the functional form of Ashby scoring.

questions.question: Q2. The Timoshenko bilayer curvature κ is linear in mismatch strain Δε. Given that finite-strain simulation produces κ_sim that deviates from the linear Timoshenko prediction as Δε increases, what is the dominant physical cause?

answers.a: Geometric nonlinearity: large bending angles render the linear differential geometry invalid.
answers.b: Material nonlinearity: the moduli E₁ and E₂ change with strain.
answers.d: The recovery ratio R_r decreases at large strain.

explanations.a: Correct - Timoshenko assumes small-strain kinematics. At large curvatures (high ΔE), the arc-length and thickness changes introduce nonlinear terms absent from the classical theory, so ε_shape rises and the verification gate may fail.
explanations.b: Incorrect - While material nonlinearity can occur, the theory.md explicitly identifies finite strain geometry as the culprit.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Friction heating in a polymer sim is negligible.
explanations.d: Incorrect - R_r is inherited from Exp 7 and is fixed, not strain-dependent here.

questions.question: Q3. Sub-Calc B inherits R_r = 92 % from Exp 1 (recovery ratio for SMP-PLA). If the recovery were 100 % instead, what would happen to the shape error ε_shape assuming the same mismatch strain?

answers.b: It would remain unchanged (R_r does not affect shape error).
answers.d: It would oscillate depending on temperature.

explanations.b: Incorrect - R_r directly scales κ_sim in the SMP-recovery path (Exp 7).
explanations.c: Correct - The theory states that incomplete recovery drags κ_sim below κ_pred; at R_r = 100 %, this drag disappears, improving the match. However, finite strain may still cause overshoot, and the two effects compete. In the limit, better recovery makes the gate easier to pass.
explanations.d: Incorrect - The model is deterministic at fixed parameters.

questions.question: Q4. In Sub-Calc C, the energy break-even N_break = (E_mould - E_print - E_program) / (E_trigger - E_actuator). What is the sign and meaning of the denominator if E_trigger = 0 (free body-heat trigger)?

answers.a: Denominator is negative; N_break is infinite; 4D never wins.
answers.b: Denominator is negative; N_break is infinite; 4D always wins.
answers.c: Denominator is positive; N_break is small; 4D wins only at low cycle counts.
answers.d: The formula undefined; a separate analysis applies.

explanations.b: Correct - If E_trigger ≈ 0, the denominator = 0 - 100 J/cycle ≈ -100, which is negative. N_break becomes negative or infinite (depending on numerator sign), meaning there is no positive cycle count at which the conventional route catches up. The 4D part always has lower total energy.
explanations.c: Incorrect - The denominator sign and magnitude differ.
explanations.d: Incorrect - The formula applies; the interpretation changes.

questions.question: Q5. The capstone lists three distinct trigger mechanisms: body-heat (~0 J), Joule heating (~200 J/cycle), and photo/magnetic (~500 J/cycle). Rank them by the break-even cycle count N_break in a biomedical stent application (smallest N_break first).

answers.c: The ranking depends on the mould cost C_mould and is application-specific.
answers.d: Photo/magnetic < Joule < body-heat (or body-heat has no finite break-even).

explanations.a: Incorrect - Joule is more expensive than Joule per the costs given.
explanations.b: Incorrect - Body-heat leads to infinite N_break (always wins), so it cannot rank in order with finite breaks.
explanations.c: Incorrect - While C_mould enters the numerator, the trigger cost is the denominator and sets the ranking unambiguously.
explanations.d: Correct - As trigger cost drops, N_break shrinks: photo/magnetic (expensive) requires high volume to beat moulding, Joule (medium cost) breaks earlier, and body-heat has no finite break-even (4D always wins). This is why biomedical (low volume, implantable, body-heat trigger) is the killer app for 4D.

questions.question: Q6. Sub-Calc D compares C_4D = rate·t_print + C_material (flat) with C_inj(N) = C_mould/N + C_marginal (falling). What happens to N_break if the mould cost C_mould is doubled (e.g., due to complex geometry)?

answers.a: N_break doubles; moulding is delayed to higher volumes.
answers.b: N_break is unchanged; cost curves are unaffected.
answers.c: N_break halves; moulding becomes cheaper at lower volumes.

explanations.a: Correct - N_break = C_mould / (C_4D - C_marginal). Doubling C_mould directly doubles N_break, so moulding amortizes its tooling over a larger volume, making 4D-printing competitive at higher production runs. This is a key insight: manufacturing complexity favors 4D at low volume.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Higher tooling costs delay moulding's advantage, not accelerate it.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Cost values are positive by definition.

questions.question: Q7. The Ashby material indices are defined so that 'larger is better'. However, in a real design, NiTi wins on M₂ (recovery index) while SMP-PLA wins on M₁ (stiffness index). What does this ranking tell us about why aerospace morphing wings prefer SMP-PU while cardiovascular stents use NiTi?

answers.a: NiTi is cheaper for medical applications.
answers.c: Aerospace requires high stiffness for aerodynamic loading; cardiovascular requires high actuation stress to open the stent.
answers.d: Morphing wings fail if they recover too much.

explanations.a: Incorrect - Cost is not part of the M indices.
explanations.c: Correct - The weighting w₁, w₂, w₃ encode the design priorities. A morphing wing must sustain flight loads (high M₁ weight), tilting the winner toward SMP materials. A stent must deploy against vessel resistance (high M₂ weight), where NiTi's exceptional recovery stress dominates. The Ashby map does not pick winners; application requirements do.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Complete recovery is desirable; morphing needs fast return to original shape.

questions.question: Q8. The capstone's final TRL assessment places biomedical stent at TRL 6, aerospace morphing at TRL 5, soft robotics at TRL 4, and consumer goods at TRL 3. Based on the design review's Sub-Calc gates, what is the most common blocking barrier preventing any of these from advancing to the next TRL rung?

answers.c: Shape verification and model-simulation mismatch (Sub-Calc B).
answers.d: Manufacturing scalability and unit-cost economics (Sub-Calc D).

explanations.b: Incorrect - Trigger energy is niche to biomedical.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Verification failures affect aerospace (TRL 5 to 6) but are not universal.
explanations.d: Correct - Consumer goods are blocked at TRL 3 by Sub-Calc D: moulding beats 4D-printing at high volume. Soft robotics (TRL 4) cannot transition to TRL 5 without repeatability & autonomy (cyclic trigger reliability from Sub-Calc C). The capstone explicitly notes that this crossover - not any physics of the material - keeps mass-market 4D goods stuck.

questions.question: Q9. The Timoshenko bilayer formula includes a dimensionless shape function φ = 3(1+m)² + (1+mn)(m² + 1/(mn)), where m = h₁/h₂ and n = E₁/E₂. As m approaches 0 (one layer becomes much thinner), what does φ approach?

answers.c: φ approaches 3 (dominated by the thicker layer).

explanations.a: Incorrect - φ is a sum of positive terms.
explanations.b: Correct - The 1/(mn) term in the second part of φ dominates as m approaches 0, causing φ to diverge to ∞. Physically, an extremely thin active layer cannot generate curvature in a thick passive layer; the geometry becomes unfavorable. This is why the Timoshenko model assumes comparable layer thicknesses.
explanations.c: Incorrect - The 3(1+m)² term does approach 3, but the 1/(mn) term inside the second bracket diverges as m approaches 0 and dominates, so φ goes to ∞, not 3.

questions.question: Q10. The capstone describes design as 'a chain of contradictions' where every sub-calc surfaces a trade-off it cannot fully resolve. Which of the following best exemplifies this philosophy?

answers.a: All of the above, and each exemplifies a trade-off that design must navigate.
answers.b: A design that passes Sub-Calc B (shape verification) may still fail Sub-Calc C (energy break-even) if the trigger cost is too high.
answers.c: Larger moulds cost more but amortize per-part cost faster (Sub-Calc D).
answers.d: Materials with high recovery stress are always heavy; materials with low recovery stress are light.

explanations.a: Correct - The capstone's defining insight is that no stage is decided in isolation. A material that wins on M₂ loses on M₁ (A). Shape verification at small strain fails at large strain (B). A free trigger saves energy but risks biocompatibility (C). Low-volume work suits 4D, mass market suits moulds (D). Each sub-calc reveals a knot that cannot be untied; design success is navigating all of them. This is why TRL placement reflects barriers, not victories.
explanations.b: Incorrect - This describes gate cascade, not a single design contradiction.
explanations.c: Incorrect - This is Sub-Calc D's fundamental crossover.
explanations.d: Incorrect - This is one trade-off, not the capstone's full philosophy.

questions.question: Q11. In the integrated design review, a printed shape is ACCEPTED only when...

explanations.a: Correct - the shape-verification error must fall below the 10% acceptance threshold.
explanations.b: Incorrect - TRL measures maturity, not a per-part pass.
explanations.c: Incorrect - zero cost is not the criterion.
explanations.d: Incorrect - N_break is an economics figure, not the shape gate.

questions.question: Q12. Why does lifecycle energy E_4D(N) = E_print + E_program + E_trigger*N reframe '4D' at the fleet level?

answers.a: Because only a single part ever matters.
answers.b: Because payoff depends on the number of transformation cycles N and production volume - it must transform economically at scale.
answers.c: Because the energy per cycle is constant and negligible.
answers.d: Because TRL already accounts for volume.

explanations.a: Incorrect - the review scales to the whole fleet.
explanations.b: Correct - the running sum over N and volume decides whether 4D beats the conventional route economically.
explanations.c: Incorrect - the per-cycle trigger energy accumulates with N.
explanations.d: Incorrect - TRL is maturity, not production volume.
